impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the six-year statute of limitations in 28 U.S.C. § 2501 for claims against the government in the Court of Federal Claims is subject to American Pipe class action tolling.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that 28 U.S.C. § 2501 is not subject to American Pipe tolling, affirming dismissal of breach of contract and Fifth Amendment takings claims by a bank holding company that lost nearly $898 million in Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac preferred shares during the 2008 financial crisis. The court recognized that its earlier decision in Bright v. United States was implicitly overruled by the Supreme Court's ANZ Securities decision.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides the government with a clear defense against stale claims, giving finality to financial crisis-era disputes and reducing exposure to late-filed suits by investors who relied on class action tolling.
impacts.negativeImplications: Investors and businesses that relied on pending class actions to toll the § 2501 limitations period may find their individual claims time-barred, eliminating the ability to recover against the government for financial crisis losses.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether copyright infringement damages against the government must be assessed by deferring to the terms of an existing license agreement, and whether the trial court's use of the 'book of wisdom' and assessment of non-compensatory damages was legally permissible.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that courts need not defer to existing license agreement terms when assessing copyright infringement damages via hypothetical negotiation, but vacated the $12.68 million damages award because the trial court adopted a legally impermissible view of the book of wisdom doctrine and assessed non-compensatory damages against the government. This case involved the DOD and DVA's unauthorized copying of TETRA® healthcare data interoperability software.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software companies and copyright holders retain the ability to argue for damages exceeding their license rates through hypothetical negotiation, rather than being capped at existing license terms.
impacts.negativeImplications: The ruling constrains damages models by prohibiting non-compensatory damages against the government and limiting improper use of hindsight in the 'book of wisdom' doctrine, potentially reducing recoverable damages in copyright infringement cases.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the three-year statute of limitations under the Defend Trade Secrets Act barred Insulet's trade secret misappropriation claim where the alleged misappropriation occurred in 2018 but suit was filed in 2023.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed a jury verdict finding trade secret misappropriation by EOFlow in developing its insulin patch pump, holding that Insulet's DTSA claim was time-barred as a matter of law. The court found that Insulet knew or should have known of the misappropriation more than three years before filing suit, despite the jury's contrary finding. This eliminated a damages award and permanent injunction against EOFlow.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides companies accused of trade secret misappropriation with a strong statute of limitations defense, reinforcing that the DTSA's three-year clock runs from when the plaintiff knew or should have known of the misappropriation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners face heightened pressure to promptly investigate and file suit upon first learning of potential misappropriation, or risk losing their claims entirely regardless of the merits.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding trade secret damages expert testimony and what damages models are permissible under the DTSA and Michigan UTSA for trade secret misappropriation.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the court to reconsider two previously excluded damages models. The court also reversed the district court's reduction of the breach of contract jury award, reinstating the original verdict. The case involved Ford's development of its own manufacturing configuration software after licensing Versata's ACM and MCA software.
impacts.positiveImplications: Trade secret plaintiffs benefit from expanded flexibility in presenting damages models, as the court directed reconsideration of previously excluded expert testimony approaches.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop competing products after licensing software face continued exposure to substantial trade secret misappropriation liability, with potentially broader damages calculations on remand.

impacts.caseName: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly applied inter partes review estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) to bar Valve from asserting invalidity grounds not included in its IPR petition.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's application of IPR estoppel against Valve, finding insufficient evidence to estop one invalidity ground and inadequate accounting for hindsight bias in estopping the other. The court clarified that the 'reasonably could have raised' standard for IPR estoppel requires careful evidentiary analysis without hindsight bias when determining what a skilled searcher would have found.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in patent litigation retain broader ability to assert invalidity defenses in district court that were not raised in IPR petitions, as the court tightened the evidentiary requirements for applying estoppel.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face greater difficulty using IPR estoppel to preclude invalidity challenges in district court, potentially increasing the cost and complexity of patent enforcement litigation.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court's use of a single verdict form question covering infringement for all asserted patents and its jury instruction on § 101 validity warranted vacatur, and whether asserted claims of wireless building automation patents survive § 101 challenges.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the $11.5 million infringement and damages judgments against ecobee and remanded for a new trial, finding that the verdict form improperly used a single question covering infringement for all four asserted patents. The court also vacated and remanded for further Alice step two proceedings on the '495 patent but affirmed that the '887 and '371 patents were not directed to abstract ideas under § 101.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants benefit from the requirement that verdict forms must separately address infringement for each asserted patent, preventing bundled verdicts that obscure which patents are actually infringed.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders with multiple asserted patents face increased trial complexity, as courts must ensure separate infringement findings for each patent, and § 101 challenges to wireless communication patents remain viable.

impacts.caseName: Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Pfizer Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a change from 'C2-C12-alkyl' to 'C1-C12-alkyl' in a patent specification constituted correction of an obvious typographical error entitled to priority from an earlier provisional application, or instead added new matter that broke the priority chain.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment invalidating Enanta's '953 patent covering coronavirus protease inhibitor compounds, holding that the change from C2 to C1 in the substituent definition was not an obvious typographical error and broke the priority chain to the provisional application. Pfizer's intervening public disclosure of nirmatrelvir (the active ingredient in Paxlovid®) therefore anticipated the patent claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic and competing pharmaceutical companies benefit from a strict standard for what constitutes an 'obvious typographical error' in priority documents, making it harder for patentees to retroactively broaden claim scope through provisional applications.
impacts.negativeImplications: Pharmaceutical companies face significant risk that minor discrepancies between provisional and non-provisional applications—even alleged typos—can destroy priority claims and render valuable patents invalid to intervening prior art.

impacts.caseName: Otsuka America Pharmaceutical, Inc. v. Hetero Labs Limited
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly construed 'dextromethorphan' and 'quinidine' in a pharmaceutical patent's weight-to-weight ratio limitation, and whether the court could waive the Rule 65(c) bond requirement pending appeal of a preliminary injunction.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed a preliminary injunction blocking Hetero from launching a generic competitor to Nuedexta but vacated the district court's waiver of the Rule 65(c) bond requirement pending appeal. The court upheld the claim construction that the weight-to-weight ratio refers to the active moieties rather than salt forms, sustaining a finding of likely infringement.
impacts.positiveImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies can obtain preliminary injunctions against generic competitors based on patent claims specifying drug weight ratios, with the court adopting a construction favoring broader patent scope.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic pharmaceutical companies face injunctions blocking market entry, though the ruling requiring a bond pending appeal provides some financial protection if the injunction is later reversed.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents directed to automated systems for capturing, processing, and sharing farming data using relay devices on farming equipment claim patent-eligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the case was exceptional under § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's farming data collection patents were directed to patent-ineligible abstract ideas under § 101, but vacated the district court's determination that the case was not exceptional under § 285, remanding for reconsideration of Farmers Edge's attorneys' fees request. The court found the claims were directed to the abstract idea of collecting, processing, and sharing farming data using conventional technology.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies in agriculture and IoT benefit from continued enforcement of § 101 against broadly-claimed data collection and processing patents, reducing exposure to infringement suits based on abstract data handling concepts.
impacts.negativeImplications: AgTech patent holders face heightened risk that patents claiming automated data collection and processing using sensors and GPS on farming equipment will be invalidated under § 101, and may also face attorneys' fees exposure.

impacts.caseName: Board of Regents of the University of Texas v. Boston Scientific Corp.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Boston Scientific was entitled to judgment as a matter of law of invalidity for anticipation and non-infringement of claims covering drug-releasing biodegradable fiber implant compositions used in coronary stent systems.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury's infringement verdict in favor of the University of Texas, holding that Boston Scientific was entitled to JMOL of both invalidity for anticipation and non-infringement of the '296 patent covering drug-eluting stent technology. The court found prior art anticipated the asserted claims and that BSC's products did not infringe, eliminating UT's damages award.
impacts.positiveImplications: Medical device companies benefit from a strong anticipation defense, as the court was willing to overturn a jury verdict finding infringement where prior art clearly anticipated the claimed compositions.
impacts.negativeImplications: University patent holders and research institutions face challenges enforcing broadly-claimed biomedical composition patents against established medical device manufacturers when relevant prior art exists.

impacts.caseName: TrackTime, LLC v. Amazon.com Services LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claim terms reciting 'executable program code configured to' perform functions in software patents should be treated as means-plus-function terms under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f), in light of the court's intervening precedent in Dyfan v. Target Corp.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's indefiniteness ruling on the '978 patent and remanded for reconsideration in light of Dyfan, finding that the district court's treatment of 'executable program code configured to' limitations as means-plus-function terms warranted fresh analysis under intervening precedent. The court affirmed the invalidity finding for the '638 patent on anticipation grounds.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software patent holders benefit from the opportunity to argue that 'executable program code' claim terms recite sufficient structure to avoid means-plus-function treatment under the Dyfan framework, potentially saving claims from indefiniteness.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies defending against software patent assertions face uncertainty as courts reconsider how broadly 'executable program code' limitations invoke § 112(f), potentially reviving previously invalidated claims.

impacts.caseName: KG Dongbu Steel Co., Ltd. v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Court of International Trade properly sustained Commerce's remand determination that three government-directed debt-to-equity conversions conferred no countervailable benefit to a Korean steel producer.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade and instructed reinstatement of Commerce's original determinations that the debt-to-equity conversions conferred countervailable benefits. The court held that Commerce's original methodology for evaluating whether equity infusions by the Korean government were inconsistent with usual private investor practices should be reinstated, rejecting Commerce's protest remand determination.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic steel producers and manufacturers benefit from stronger enforcement of countervailing duty laws, as Commerce's original subsidy determinations are reinstated, leveling the competitive playing field against subsidized imports.
impacts.negativeImplications: Foreign producers and importers of steel products face increased countervailing duties and reduced ability to challenge Commerce's subsidy determinations through iterative remand proceedings.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that grants an exclusive license but retains the right to sue third parties for infringement has sufficient constitutional standing to bring a patent infringement action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed dismissal for lack of standing, holding that patent owners who retain the right to sue third parties for infringement maintain a non-illusory exclusionary right sufficient to satisfy Article III standing, even after granting an exclusive license. The court found that A.L.M.'s retained enforcement rights, combined with sublicensing approval rights and restrictions on assignment, preserved sufficient injury-in-fact.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners structuring license agreements can retain enforcement standing by preserving the right to sue infringers, providing flexibility to monetize patents through licensing while maintaining independent enforcement capability.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers face broader standing for patent enforcement actions, as patent owners with retained litigation rights can independently bring suit even after granting exclusive commercial licenses.

impacts.caseName: mCom IP, LLC v. City National Bank of Florida
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court properly dismissed patent infringement claims on obviousness grounds at the pleading stage and whether the case qualified as exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285 warranting attorneys' fees and sanctions under 28 U.S.C. § 1927.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed dismissal of patent infringement claims for the '508 patent (unified electronic banking system) on obviousness grounds but reversed the § 285 exceptional case fee award and § 1927 sanctions against counsel. The court found that while the infringement complaint was properly dismissed, the grounds presented were insufficient to support a finding that the case was exceptional or that counsel acted in bad faith.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent litigators and their clients benefit from a higher threshold for exceptional case findings and attorney sanctions, reducing the chilling effect on patent enforcement even when claims are ultimately unsuccessful.
impacts.negativeImplications: Defendants who successfully defeat patent claims at the pleading stage face greater difficulty recovering attorneys' fees, even when the asserted patents had been largely invalidated in IPR proceedings.

impacts.caseName: Wyeth LLC v. AstraZeneca Pharmaceuticals LP
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming methods of treating gefitinib/erlotinib-resistant non-small cell lung cancer with irreversible EGFR inhibitors were invalid as a matter of law.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed JMOL of invalidity for Wyeth's patents covering methods of treating drug-resistant lung cancer with irreversible EGFR inhibitors. The decision impacts pharmaceutical patent strategy for claiming therapeutic methods directed at overcoming drug resistance, affirming that broadly-claimed treatment methods may be vulnerable to invalidity challenges.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic and competing pharmaceutical companies can more confidently develop irreversible EGFR inhibitor products without fear of infringement liability from broadly-claimed cancer treatment method patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Pharmaceutical innovators face increased difficulty obtaining and enforcing method-of-treatment patents that broadly claim the use of a class of compounds for treating drug-resistant cancers.
